objective: By the end of this lesson you can say who is responsible for an aircraft's airworthiness, check that every required document is on board and current, and read the maintenance records well enough to decide whether a given aircraft may fly.
why: Rules on registration and records have changed in recent years, and an expired registration or a missing return-to-service entry grounds an airplane that looks perfect on the ramp. The PIC is the last person who can catch it.

warmup: You show up to rent an airplane you have never flown. Before you touch the airframe, which pieces of paper would you look for, and what on each one could ground the airplane?

key_terms.def: The aircraft conforms to its type design and is in condition for safe operation.
White certificate for normal, utility, acrobatic, commuter and transport category aircraft. Must be displayed in the aircraft.
Pink certificate for primary, restricted, limited, light-sport, experimental aircraft and special flight permits.
FAA certificate issued to the owner. Now expires seven years after the last day of the month it was issued.
The second copy of the Aircraft Registration Application, carried by a new owner. Valid only within the United States.
Limits in the approved AFM, markings and placards that every flight must comply with (91.9).
FAA-approved flight manual for one specific aircraft, identified by serial number and registration on the title page.
Signed record entry by an authorized person after maintenance. Required before the aircraft may fly.
Part with a mandatory replacement time. Its current status is a required owner record (91.417(a)(2)(ii)).
Major Repair and Alteration form. Copies are kept with the records; one must be aboard for a cabin or baggage fuel tank.

chunks.title: Who decides the airplane is airworthy

body.p: Two short rules split the job. 91.7(a): no person may operate a civil aircraft unless it is in an airworthy condition. 91.7(b): the PIC is responsible for determining whether the aircraft is in condition for safe flight, and must discontinue the flight when unairworthy mechanical, electrical or structural conditions occur [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]].
"Airworthy" has two parts: the aircraft conforms to its type design, and it is in condition for safe operation [[24:38|AFH 2-1]].

head: Who
Rule
What it means for you
rows: Primarily responsible for maintaining the aircraft airworthy, including compliance with part 39 (ADs) [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]]
Arranges inspections, repairs and records. Renters and club members rely on this work.
Determines whether the aircraft is in condition for safe flight, and discontinues the flight if it becomes unairworthy [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]]
You make the final call, every flight, even in someone else's airplane.
May not operate an aircraft that is not airworthy [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(a)]]
Applies to whoever flies it, whatever the owner says.

body.p: Inoperative equipment is part of this. Unless an item is covered by an approved MEL or the relief in 91.213(d) or (e), an inoperative item on the aircraft is a violation of 91.7 [[58:7|AC 91-67A 1.7.1]]. The inoperative equipment lesson covers those steps.

callout.text: Common mistake: "The FBO maintains it, so airworthiness is their problem." The owner or operator is primarily responsible for maintenance, but under 91.7(a) and (b) you as PIC still decide whether this airplane is in condition for safe flight today [[24:38|AFH 2-1]].

check.q: You rent an airplane the flight school maintains. Who decides whether it is safe for your flight today?
check.a: You, the PIC, under 91.7(b) [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]]. The school, as operator, is primarily responsible for maintaining it [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]].

chunks.title: What the owner or operator must do

body.p: Under 91.405, each owner or operator must [[60:520|14 CFR 91.405(a)]] [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(b)-(d)]]:

bullets: Have the aircraft inspected as subpart E requires, and between inspections have discrepancies repaired under part 43.
Make sure maintenance personnel make record entries approving the aircraft for return to service.
Have any item left inoperative under 91.213(d)(2) repaired, replaced, removed or inspected at the next required inspection.
Make sure a placard is installed when listed discrepancies include inoperative instruments or equipment.

body.p: 91.403 adds two more. Maintenance must follow subpart E and part 43 [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(b)]]. And if the maintenance manual or instructions for continued airworthiness have an airworthiness limitations section, its mandatory replacement times and inspection intervals must be met before anyone may operate the aircraft [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(c)]].

The PHAK sums up the owner's job: keep a current airworthiness certificate and registration in the aircraft, keep it airworthy including all ADs, make sure maintenance is properly recorded, keep up with current rules, and notify the FAA Aircraft Registry of a change of address, a sale or export, or loss of eligibility to register [[1:243|PHAK 9-13]].

callout.text: After maintenance, no person may operate the aircraft until it has been approved for return to service by an authorized person and the 43.9 or 43.11 record entry has been made [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]]. If the work may have appreciably changed flight characteristics, no passengers may be carried until a pilot with at least a private certificate flies an operational check and logs it in the aircraft records, unless ground tests or inspection show conclusively that nothing changed [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(b)-(c)]].

check.q: A mechanic re-rigged the ailerons yesterday. The return-to-service entry is signed. What does 91.407(b) require before you take a passenger?
check.a: If the work may have appreciably changed flight characteristics, a pilot with at least a private certificate flies the airplane, makes an operational check and logs the flight in the aircraft records, unless ground tests or inspection show conclusively that nothing changed [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(b)-(c)]].

chunks.title: Documents that must be in the aircraft

body.p: 91.203(a) says no person may operate a civil aircraft unless it has within it an appropriate and current airworthiness certificate [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)(1)]] and an effective U.S. registration certificate issued to its owner, or, for operation within the United States, the second copy of the Aircraft Registration Application under 47.31(c) [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(a)(2)]].
The AFH list of what must be on board, attached or affixed, as appropriate [[24:41|AFH 2-4]]:

head: Item
Source rule
Notes
rows: Displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance, legible to passengers or crew [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(b)]]
Effective, and issued to the current owner [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(a)(2)]]
AFM/POH, placards, instrument markings, or a combination [[24:41|AFH 2-4]]
Use the most current data [[22:18|W&B Handbook 1-4]]
If required under the applicable standards [[24:41|AFH 2-4]]
FAA Form 337 for a cabin or baggage fuel tank
Only if such a tank is installed [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(c)]]
Only for flights outside the United States or airplanes over 12,500 pounds [[24:41|AFH 2-4]]

callout.text: Many pilots learned ARROW: Airworthiness certificate, Registration, Radio station license, Operating limitations, Weight and balance. It still works if you remember the radio license is only for flights outside the United States or airplanes over 12,500 pounds [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

Common mistake: thinking the logbooks must ride in the airplane. 91.203 does not list them, and logbooks are not normally kept in the airplane. Inspect them, or a summary of airworthy status, before flight [[24:39|AFH 2-2]].

check.q: Which item on the ARROW list is not needed for a local flight in a 2,500-pound airplane?
check.a: The FCC radio station license. It applies to flights outside the United States or airplanes over 12,500 pounds [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

chunks.title: Registration: Part 47 as it reads now

body.p: No person may operate an aircraft eligible for U.S. registration unless its owner has registered it, or it carries the temporary authorization of 47.31(c) [[60:156|14 CFR 47.3(b)]]. Registration is not proof of ownership; the FAA issues no certificate of ownership [[60:156|14 CFR 47.5(c)]].

head: Topic
Current rule
rows: Expires seven years after the last day of the month in which it is issued [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40(a)]]
File AC Form 8050-1B and the fee during the six months before the expiration date [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40(b)]]
Revoked, canceled or ownership transferred; registered in a foreign country; totally destroyed or scrapped; holder loses U.S. citizenship; 30 days after the holder's death [[60:169|14 CFR 47.41(a)]]

Notice within 21 days in most cases: by email for an electronic certificate, or by returning a paper certificate with the back completed. An expired paper certificate is destroyed [[60:169|14 CFR 47.41(b)]]
Notify the Registry in writing within 30 days [[60:170|14 CFR 47.45]]
Carries the second copy of the Aircraft Registration Application as temporary authority, within the United States only [[60:166|14 CFR 47.31(c)]]

callout.text: Changed: 47.40 was rewritten by an amendment published November 22, 2022 and revised January 17, 2025 [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40]]. A registration certificate now expires seven years after the last day of its month of issue. If you learned a shorter period, it is out of date. The PHAK sample in Figure 9-8 is a 1995 form with only a date of issue [[1:236|PHAK 9-6]], so read the expiration date on the real certificate.

Changed: the PHAK still says the pink copy of the application allows operation for up to 90 days [[1:237|PHAK 9-7]]. The current 47.31(c) makes the second copy valid within the United States until you receive the certificate or the FAA denies the application. It is not available once 12 months have passed since the Registry received the first application after the transfer, and it cannot be used if no registration number has been assigned [[60:166|14 CFR 47.31(c)]].

body.p: Example: issued March 10, 2026. The last day of that month is March 31, 2026, so it expires March 31, 2033 [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40(a)]]. The renewal window is the six months before that date [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40(b)]].

check.q: A registration certificate was issued April 18, 2026. When does it expire?
check.a: April 30, 2033: seven years after the last day of the month of issue [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40(a)]].

body.p: An FAA representative issues the airworthiness certificate after the aircraft is inspected, found to meet part 21 and in condition for safe operation. It stays with the aircraft unless the aircraft is sold to a foreign purchaser [[1:237|PHAK 9-7]].

bullets: It must carry the aircraft's registration number (special flight permits and a few others excepted) [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)(1)]].
It must be displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance so it is legible to passengers or crew [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(b)]].
Box 4, Category, is the category whose limitations the aircraft must be operated under [[1:237|PHAK 9-7]].

head: Kind
Color
Issued for
rows: Normal, utility, acrobatic, commuter or transport category aircraft, manned free balloons and special class aircraft [[1:73|PHAK 3-2]]
Primary, restricted, limited, light-sport, provisional, special flight permits (ferry permits) and experimental [[1:73|PHAK 3-2]]

body.p: How long is it good? Standard certificates are effective as long as the aircraft is registered in the United States and maintenance, preventive maintenance and alterations are done under parts 43 and 91 [[60:66|14 CFR 21.181(a)]] [[60:67|14 CFR 21.181(a)(1)]]. A special flight permit is effective only for the period it states [[60:67|14 CFR 21.181(a)(2)]].

callout.text: Common mistake: "The airworthiness certificate never expires." It has no expiration date, but it is effective only while the aircraft is registered in the United States and properly maintained [[60:66|14 CFR 21.181(a)]] [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. Let the registration lapse and the airworthiness certificate stops being effective too.

check.q: The airworthiness certificate in the airplane shows N2631A, but the airplane is painted N2613A. What rule does this break?
check.a: 91.203(a)(1): the airworthiness certificate must have on it the registration number assigned to that aircraft [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)(1)]]. Don't fly until it is sorted out.

chunks.title: Operating limitations: AFM, markings and placards

body.p: No person may operate a civil aircraft without complying with the operating limitations in the approved flight manual, markings and placards [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9(a)]]. If 21.5 requires a flight manual, a current approved one must be available in the aircraft. If not, a current approved AFM, approved manual material, markings and placards, or a combination, must be available [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9(b)]].

21.5 covers airplanes not type certificated with a flight manual that had no flight time before March 1, 1979: they are delivered with a current approved AFM [[60:34|14 CFR 21.5(a)]]. The POH for most light airplanes built after 1975 is also the FAA-approved flight manual [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]].

callout.text: Common mistake: flying with a generic owner's or information manual. It is not FAA approved, not specific to one aircraft, not kept current, and cannot be substituted for the AFM/POH. A real AFM/POH has the serial number and registration on its title page; without them it is for general study only [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]].

head: Airspeed marking
Meaning
rows: Never-exceed speed (VNE). Structural damage could occur beyond it [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]]
VNO to VNE. Smooth air only, and then only with caution [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]]
Normal operating range, from VS1 up to VNO [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]]
Flap operating range, from VS0 up to VFE [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]]

body.p: Engine gauges show limits too: a red radial line for the maximum or minimum limit and a green arc for the normal range [[1:233|PHAK 9-3]]. Placards with a direct bearing on safe operation are posted in conspicuous places and reproduced in the Limitations section, or required by an AD [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]].
Last, the aircraft must be identified under part 45 or 48 [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9(c)]], including the external data plate [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

check.q: Your rental first flew in 1985 and its type certificate came without a flight manual, so 21.5 applies. Only a generic information manual with no serial number is aboard. Can you go?
check.a: No. An information manual cannot substitute for the AFM/POH [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]], and an airplane covered by 21.5 must have a current approved flight manual available in it [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9(b)(1)]].

chunks.title: Weight and balance data and the equipment list

body.p: The Limitations section gives the maximum certificated weights and the CG range. The Weight and Balance/Equipment List section holds everything the FAA requires to calculate weight and balance [[1:233|PHAK 9-3]] [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]].

The equipment list in the AFM/POH identifies the items required for airworthiness, plus optional and supplemental items [[24:25|AFH 1-4]]. When a mechanic adds or removes equipment, the new empty weight and empty-weight CG are recorded in the weight and balance record and the equipment list is updated [[22:17|W&B Handbook 1-3]] [[22:30|W&B Handbook 2-10]].

callout.text: The mechanic doing an annual or condition inspection must make sure the weight and balance data in the aircraft records is current and accurate. The PIC is responsible for using the most current weight and balance data when operating the aircraft [[22:18|W&B Handbook 1-4]].
After any avionics or interior change, look for a weight and balance report dated after the work. Extra radios and instruments have overloaded many aircraft [[22:17|W&B Handbook 1-3]].

check.q: The POH has the factory weight and balance sheet, but the logbook shows a new autopilot installed last year with a revised weight and balance. Which do you use?
check.a: The revised one. The PIC must use the most current weight and balance data [[22:18|W&B Handbook 1-4]].

body.p: 91.417(a)(1): the registered owner or operator keeps records of maintenance, preventive maintenance, alterations and required inspections for the airframe, each engine, propeller and appliance. Each record shows a description of the work, the date it was completed, and the signature and certificate number of the person approving return to service [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(1)]].

head: 91.417(a)(2) record
What it shows
rows: Hours on the airframe, each engine and each propeller
Current status of each life-limited part
Time since last overhaul of items that must be overhauled on a time basis
Current status, including time since the last required inspection
Each applicable AD: number, revision date, method of compliance, and the time and date of the next action if it recurs
Copies of the Form 337 for each major alteration to the airframe and installed engines, propellers and appliances

body.p: All of these come from [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(2)]].

head: Record
How long it is kept
rows: Until the work is repeated or superseded, or 1 year after the work [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(1)]]
Kept and transferred with the aircraft when it is sold [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(2)]] [[60:527|14 CFR 91.419]]
List of defects from an inspection
Until the defects are repaired and the aircraft is approved for return to service [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(3)]]

body.p: The owner must make the records available to the FAA or the NTSB, and show the cabin fuel tank Form 337 to a law enforcement officer on request [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(c)]]. An inspection entry states the type and extent of the inspection, the date, total time in service and the signer's certificate, and either certifies the aircraft airworthy or says a list of discrepancies was given to the owner [[60:134|14 CFR 43.11(a)]].

A recurring AD might require an inspection every 50 hours of time in service. There is no provision to overfly an AD's hour limit unless the AD itself allows it [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]]. Logbooks usually come as airframe and engine books, sometimes with propeller and appliance books [[24:39|AFH 2-2]].

check.q: The annual entry says "a list of discrepancies and unairworthy items dated ... has been provided." May the airplane fly?
check.a: Not yet. That wording means it was not approved for return to service [[60:134|14 CFR 43.11(a)(5)]]. The owner keeps the list until the defects are repaired and the aircraft is approved for return to service [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(3)]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: the document check

body.p: Do this before the walk-around, every time you fly an unfamiliar or shared airplane. The AFH puts the records review first, then the visual inspection [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

bullets: 1. Registration: N-number matches, owner is current, expiration date not passed [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40(a)]]. New owner? Look for the second copy of the application, and stay in the United States [[60:166|14 CFR 47.31(c)]].
2. Airworthiness certificate: displayed at the entrance, N-number matches [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)(1)]] [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(b)]].
3. Aircraft identification: N-number and data plate match the documents [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9(c)]] [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].
4. AFM/POH: this aircraft's serial number and registration on the title page, with supplements for installed equipment [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]] [[1:235|PHAK 9-5]].
5. Weight and balance: the latest report, then your loading for today [[22:18|W&B Handbook 1-4]].
6. Logbooks or status summary: inspections current, AD status, and a return-to-service entry after the latest work [[24:40|AFH 2-3]] [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]].
7. Any discrepancy: address it before flight. Then start the visual preflight [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

callout.text: On a practical test you are asked to produce and explain the registration, airworthiness certificate, operating limitations or AFM, equipment list, weight and balance data, maintenance records and applicable ADs [[1:38|PHAK 1-23]]. Expect the same at a flight review.

check.q: Documents and logbooks check out. What is next?
check.a: The visual preflight inspection, starting as you walk up to the airplane [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

chunks.title: Risk: expired registration or missing documents

body.p: Missing or lapsed paperwork is not a technicality. Without an effective registration (or valid temporary authority) and a current airworthiness certificate on board, no person may operate the aircraft [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)]] [[60:156|14 CFR 47.3(b)]].

Registration can end with nobody touching the airplane: the expiration date passes, the airplane is sold, or the holder dies [[60:169|14 CFR 47.41(a)]]. Shared, club and newly bought airplanes are where this bites.

callout.text: Common mistake: "It's only paperwork, the airplane is fine." An expired registration grounds the aircraft, and the airworthiness certificate is effective only as long as the aircraft is registered in the United States [[60:66|14 CFR 21.181(a)]].

body.p: Use PAVE. Paperwork is an Aircraft hazard. The usual trap is an External pressure: passengers waiting, a schedule to keep. Ask why the flight is being made, how critical the schedule is, and whether the trip is worth the risk [[30:11|RMH 1-2]].

bullets: Read the expiration date on the registration every time you fly a shared airplane.
Owners: file renewal during the six-month window before expiration [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40(b)]], and tell the Registry of an address change within 30 days [[60:170|14 CFR 47.45]].
Buying an airplane: carry the second copy of your application and stay within the United States until the certificate arrives [[60:166|14 CFR 47.31(c)]].

check.q: Your passengers are loaded when you notice the registration expired last month. What do you do?
check.a: Don't fly. No one may operate it without an effective registration [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(a)(2)]], and the airworthiness certificate is no longer effective either [[60:66|14 CFR 21.181(a)]]. Resist the external pressure [[30:11|RMH 1-2]].

scenario.title: The club airplane before your flight review
scenario.setup: Today is October 20, 2026. You meet your CFI at 0800 for a flight review in your flying club's Piper Archer. Two club members are waiting to fly it at 1100. In the document pouch you find the registration certificate in the club's name with an expiration date of August 31, 2026, the airworthiness certificate folded in a plastic sleeve, and the POH. The logbooks are in the club office. The latest airframe entry is the annual from five months ago, signed by an IA, followed by a mechanic's entry from last week for a new transponder.

questions.q: Can you fly the flight review in this airplane today?
questions.a: No. The registration expired August 31, 2026 [[60:169|14 CFR 47.41(a)]], and no person may operate the aircraft without an effective registration [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(a)(2)]] [[60:156|14 CFR 47.3(b)]]. The airworthiness certificate is effective only while the aircraft is registered [[60:66|14 CFR 21.181(a)]].

questions.q: A club member says, "Nobody checks that. We fly it all the time." How do you think about this?
questions.a: That is an External pressure in PAVE. Ask why the flight is being made and whether it is worth the risk [[30:11|RMH 1-2]]. As PIC you decide, and the rule says no person may operate it [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)]].

questions.q: How should the club have prevented this?
questions.a: The registered owner could have filed AC Form 8050-1B and the fee during the six months before August 31, 2026 [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40(b)]]. The owner is responsible for keeping a current registration in the aircraft [[1:243|PHAK 9-13]].

questions.q: Suppose the registration were current. Is the airworthiness certificate in the sleeve OK as it is?
questions.a: Only if it is displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance so passengers or crew can read it [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(b)]], and it carries this aircraft's registration number [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)(1)]].

questions.q: What do you look for in the logbooks about last week's transponder work?
questions.a: An entry describing the work, the date, and the signature, certificate number and kind of certificate of the person approving it for return to service [[60:132|14 CFR 43.9(a)]]. Without it, nobody may fly the airplane [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]]. Also check that the weight and balance and equipment list were updated if they changed [[22:30|W&B Handbook 2-10]].

skills.do: Given an aircraft, find and check its registration (owner, N-number, expiration), airworthiness certificate (displayed, number matches), operating limitations (this aircraft's AFM/POH, markings, placards), current weight and balance data, and the maintenance records (inspection and AD status, return to service after the latest work), then say whether it may fly and why.
skills.practice: Before your next flight review, run the seven-step document check on the airplane you'll fly and explain each item to your CFI, as the PHAK practical test list expects [[1:38|PHAK 1-23]]. Use the AFH airworthiness checklist as a model [[24:40|AFH 2-3]].

quiz.q: Under 14 CFR 91.403(a), who is primarily responsible for maintaining an aircraft in airworthy condition, including AD compliance?
options: The pilot in command
The owner or operator
The mechanic who did the last annual
The FAA
quiz.why: 91.403(a) puts it on the owner or operator [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]]. The PIC decides whether it is safe for each flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]].

quiz.q: In flight, a structural problem makes the airplane unairworthy. What does 91.7(b) require?
options: Continue if the airplane still handles normally
Report it after landing at your destination
Discontinue the flight
Declare an emergency and continue
quiz.why: The PIC shall discontinue the flight when unairworthy mechanical, electrical or structural conditions occur [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]].

quiz.q: Where must the airworthiness certificate be?
options: Displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance, legible to passengers or crew
Anywhere in the aircraft, such as the glovebox
With the logbooks in the owner's office
In the POH, inside the front cover
quiz.why: 91.203(b) requires it to be displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance so it is legible to passengers or crew [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(b)]].

quiz.q: Under the current 47.40(a), a Certificate of Aircraft Registration expires:
options: Three years after the date of issue
Five years after the date of issue
Never, unless the aircraft is sold
Seven years after the last day of the month of issue
quiz.why: It expires seven years after the last day of the month in which it is issued [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40(a)]].

quiz.q: What does the second copy of the Aircraft Registration Application allow the new owner to do?
options: Operate anywhere for 90 days
Operate within the United States until the certificate arrives or the application is denied
Operate within the United States for 30 days
Nothing; the aircraft may not fly until the certificate arrives
quiz.why: 47.31(c)(1) makes it temporary authority within the United States until the certificate is received or the FAA denies the application [[60:166|14 CFR 47.31(c)]]. The PHAK's 90 days is outdated [[1:237|PHAK 9-7]].

quiz.q: A standard airworthiness certificate stays effective as long as:
options: It is renewed at each annual inspection
The owner holds a current pilot certificate
The aircraft is registered in the U.S. and maintained under parts 43 and 91
It is less than 10 years old
quiz.why: 21.181(a) ties it to U.S. registration and maintenance under parts 43 and 91 [[60:66|14 CFR 21.181(a)]] [[60:67|14 CFR 21.181(a)(1)]].

quiz.q: Which statement about a manufacturer's generic information manual is correct?
options: It may replace the AFM/POH if the airplane is older than 1975
It is FAA approved but not kept current
It is fine for flight if the placards are installed
It is not FAA approved and cannot be substituted for the AFM/POH
quiz.why: The information manual is not FAA approved, not specific to one aircraft, not kept current and cannot be substituted for the AFM/POH [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]].

quiz.q: Who is responsible for using the most current weight and balance data when operating the aircraft?
options: The PIC
The mechanic who did the last annual
The registered owner only
The aircraft manufacturer
quiz.why: The mechanic keeps the data current at inspections, but the PIC must use the most current data [[22:18|W&B Handbook 1-4]].

quiz.q: Which records must be transferred with the aircraft when it is sold?
options: Only the last annual inspection entry
None; the seller may keep all records
The 91.417(a)(2) status records, such as total time and AD status
Only records less than 1 year old
quiz.why: The (a)(2) records are retained and transferred with the aircraft at the time of sale [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(2)]] [[60:527|14 CFR 91.419(a)]].

takeaways: Owner or operator maintains it (91.403). The PIC decides it is safe for each flight and stops if it isn't (91.7).
On board: airworthiness certificate (displayed), effective registration, operating limitations, current weight and balance. Logbooks stay with the owner.
Registration now expires seven years after the last day of the month of issue. Renew in the six months before.
A new owner's second copy of the application works only within the U.S., until the certificate arrives or is denied. The PHAK's 90 days is outdated.
No registration means no effective airworthiness certificate (21.181).
Use this aircraft's AFM/POH, not a generic manual, and the latest weight and balance report.
Records show the work, who approved it, total time, life-limited parts, inspection and AD status. No return-to-service entry, no flight.
cfi_notes: PHAK 9-7 still says the pink copy of the registration application allows operation for 90 days. The current 14 CFR 47.31(c) has no 90-day limit: valid within the U.S. until the certificate arrives or is denied, and not available 12 months after the Registry received the first application. Teach the regulation.

PHAK Figure 9-8 is a 1995 registration form with no expiration date, and PHAK 9-6 tells owners to mail the certificate back. 47.41(b) now allows email notice for electronically issued certificates and says to destroy an expired paper one. Have students look at a real current certificate.
Pilots often remember an older, shorter registration period. 47.40 now gives seven years after the last day of the month of issue. Make students compute an expiration date from a real certificate.
Examiners commonly probe the link between registration and the airworthiness certificate (21.181(a)). Ask: "The registration lapsed last week. Is the airworthiness certificate still effective?"

PHAK 9-12 says the AD record includes the signature and certificate number of the person who did the work. 91.417(a)(2)(v) itself lists AD number, revision date, method of compliance and next due time; the signature requirement comes from (a)(1)(iii) and 43.9. Point students to the rule text.
Students often think logbooks must be aboard. Show them 91.203 and AFH 2-2. Then make them actually review the logbooks before the flight review, since PIC responsibility (91.7(b)) still applies.

ARROW is a handy memory aid, but stress that the radio station license applies only outside the U.S. or over 12,500 pounds (AFH 2-4), and that ARROW leaves out the data plate, compass card and any Form 337 for a cabin fuel tank.
gaps: 14 CFR part 3 (the definition of airworthy) and part 45 (identification and data plate) are not in the uploaded set; the lesson uses the AFH's description of them.
The sources do not give the registration period that applied before the 2022 rewrite of 47.40, so the lesson only says older, shorter periods are out of date.
No source explains how an electronically issued registration certificate should be carried or shown in the aircraft, or whether copies of certificates are acceptable.
FCC radio station license rules are not in the sources beyond the one AFH line.
A specific aircraft's required equipment, placards and limitations come from its own AFM/POH and type certificate data sheet, not this lesson.

activities.title: Owner or PIC: who has to do what?
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: If the flight school maintains a rental airplane, the renter pilot is no longer responsible for its airworthiness.
cards.why: False. The PIC is responsible for determining whether the aircraft is in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]].

cards.s: The owner or operator is primarily responsible for AD compliance.
cards.why: True. 91.403(a) includes compliance with part 39 [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]].

cards.s: Between required inspections, the owner must have discrepancies repaired under part 43.
Once the mechanic finishes the work, the airplane may fly even if the logbook entry is made later.
cards.why: False. The approval for return to service and the 43.9 or 43.11 entry must come first [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]].

cards.s: If the AFM's airworthiness limitations section sets a mandatory replacement time, the aircraft may not be operated past it.
If an unairworthy mechanical condition occurs in flight, the PIC may press on to the destination as long as the airplane is controllable.
cards.why: False. The PIC shall discontinue the flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]].

activities.title: In the airplane, or with the owner?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.
buckets: Owner keeps it; not required on board

items.t: Form 337 for a fuel tank installed in the baggage compartment
Copies of Form 337 for a major alteration to the panel

activities.title: Part 47 timelines
activities.intro: Tap a rule, then tap what it says.

pairs.r: Seven years after the last day of the month issued
The six months before the expiration date
Notify the Registry in writing within 30 days
Return it to the Registry within 21 days
Temporary authority, within the United States only

activities.title: Read the airspeed limits
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Yellow arc: smooth air only, with caution
Top of the green arc: VNO

activities.title: Dates and hours in the records
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: A Certificate of Aircraft Registration was issued June 14, 2021. In what year does it expire?
items.why: The last day of the month of issue is June 30, 2021. Seven years later is June 30, 2028 [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40(a)]].

items.q: A recurring AD requires an inspection every 50 hours of time in service. It was last done at 2,961.3 hours. The airplane now shows 3,004.8 hours. How many hours can it fly before the next inspection is due?
items.why: Next due: 2,961.3 + 50 = 3,011.3 hours. Remaining: 3,011.3 - 3,004.8 = 6.5 hours. There is no provision to overfly the AD's limit unless the AD allows it [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]], and the record must show when the next action is due [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(2)(v)]].

items.q: The engine was overhauled and installed when the airframe had 1,850.0 hours total time in service. The airframe now has 3,105.4 hours. What is the engine's time since overhaul, in hours?
items.why: 3,105.4 - 1,850.0 = 1,255.4 hours. Time since last overhaul is one of the status records the owner must keep [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(a)(2)(iii)]].

items.q: An owner moves to a new mailing address on September 12. What is the latest day in October by which the Registry must be notified?
items.why: 30 days after September 12: 18 days to September 30, then 12 more, so October 12 [[60:170|14 CFR 47.45]].

activities.title: Can I legally fly my friend's new airplane?
activities.intro: Your friend bought a Cessna 172, N4321K, two weeks ago. It first flew in 1985 and its type certificate came without a flight manual, so 14 CFR 21.5 applies. He asks you to fly it with him to lunch, and maybe on to Canada in the afternoon. You start your document check at the airplane.

steps.s: The registration certificate in the pouch is in the seller's name and does not expire until 2029.
options: Fly. The certificate has not expired yet
Ask for the second copy of the Aircraft Registration Application your friend sent to the Registry
Fly. Registration isn't needed for a private Part 91 flight
Cancel. A newly sold airplane can't fly until the new certificate arrives
steps.why: The sale ended the seller's registration [[60:169|14 CFR 47.41(a)]]. The new owner's second copy of the application serves as temporary authority [[60:166|14 CFR 47.31(c)]] [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(a)(2)]].

steps.s: He hands you the second copy of his application, sent to the Registry 13 days ago. The airplane has its assigned N-number. What about the afternoon leg to Canada?
options: Fine, temporary authority works anywhere
Keep the flight within the United States
Fine, if you also carry the seller's certificate
Fine, if you file an international flight plan
steps.why: Temporary authority is valid only for operation within the United States [[60:166|14 CFR 47.31(c)(1)]] [[1:237|PHAK 9-7]].

steps.s: The airworthiness certificate is folded in the glovebox. Its N-number matches the airplane.
options: Leave it there, it is in the aircraft
Display it at the cabin or cockpit entrance, legible to passengers or crew
Get a new one, folding voids it
Ignore it, the registration is what matters
steps.why: 91.203(b) requires it to be displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance so it is legible [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(b)]].

steps.s: The only manual aboard is a generic Cessna 172 information manual with no serial number. The real POH is at your friend's house, 20 minutes away.
options: Go. The placards and markings are enough
Go. The information manual has the same numbers
Wait while he gets this airplane's POH
Go, and download a POH from the internet on the way
steps.why: Under 21.5 this airplane was delivered with an approved flight manual [[60:34|14 CFR 21.5(a)]], so a current approved one must be in the aircraft [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9(b)(1)]]. An information manual cannot substitute for the AFM/POH [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]].

steps.s: With the POH aboard, you see the logbook entry for a new GPS installed last month, approved for return to service, with a revised weight and balance report. You load two adults and full fuel.
options: Use the factory weight and balance in the POH
Use the revised report from last month
Skip the calculation, a 172 is never over gross with two people
Average the two empty weights
steps.why: The PIC must use the most current weight and balance data [[22:18|W&B Handbook 1-4]]. Equipment changes update the empty weight and CG [[22:30|W&B Handbook 2-10]].

final_quiz.q: You buy an airplane and fly it home the same day. The seller's current registration certificate is still aboard. Is that enough?
options: Yes, until the seller's certificate expires
No. The sale ended that registration; you need the second copy of your own application
Yes, if the seller rides along
No. You must wait for the FAA to issue a special flight permit
final_quiz.why: Registration ends when ownership is transferred [[60:169|14 CFR 47.41(a)]]. The applicant carries the second copy of the application as temporary authority [[60:166|14 CFR 47.31(c)]].

final_quiz.q: The registration expired on September 30. It is now October 20. The annual is current and the airplane is in great shape. Which is true?
options: You may fly for 90 days after expiration
You may fly, since the airworthiness certificate has no expiration date
No person may operate it, and its airworthiness certificate is not effective either
You may fly solo, but not with passengers
final_quiz.why: An effective registration is required [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(a)(2)]], and the airworthiness certificate is effective only while the aircraft is registered in the U.S. [[60:66|14 CFR 21.181(a)]].

final_quiz.q: On preflight of a club airplane you find a cracked exhaust stack. The club says the mechanic will look next week and you can fly today. Who makes the call?
options: You, as PIC, decide whether it is in condition for safe flight
The club, because it is the operator
The mechanic, by phone
The last pilot who flew it
final_quiz.why: The PIC is responsible for determining whether the aircraft is in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]]. The operator's maintenance duty [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]] does not change that.

final_quiz.q: You hold a valid temporary authority (second copy of the application). Where may you fly?
options: Anywhere ICAO recognizes U.S. aircraft
Within the U.S. and Canada
Only within 50 NM of the base airport
Only within the United States
final_quiz.why: 47.31(c)(1) limits it to operation within the United States [[60:166|14 CFR 47.31(c)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: The owner keeps all the logbooks at home. The airworthiness certificate, registration, POH and weight and balance are aboard. Is the airplane legal to fly?
options: No, the logbooks must be aboard for every flight
No, a copy of the last annual must be aboard
Yes. Logbooks are not a 91.203 on-board item, though you should review them first
Yes, but only for local flights
final_quiz.why: 91.203(a) lists the airworthiness and registration certificates [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)]]. Logbooks are not normally kept in the airplane, but the pilot should review them before flight [[24:39|AFH 2-2]].

final_quiz.q: A new GPS was installed yesterday. The shop has not yet written the logbook entry. May you fly it this morning?
options: No. It needs approval for return to service and the record entry first
Yes, as long as you don't use the GPS
Yes, the work was done by a certificated shop
Yes, if you write the entry yourself
final_quiz.why: No person may operate an aircraft after maintenance or alteration until it is approved for return to service and the 43.9 or 43.11 entry is made [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]].

final_quiz.q: After flight control repairs that may have changed the handling, who may make the required check flight before passengers are carried?
options: Any student pilot with a solo endorsement
An appropriately rated pilot with at least a private certificate
Only an FAA inspector
Only the mechanic who did the work
final_quiz.why: 91.407(b) requires an appropriately rated pilot with at least a private pilot certificate to fly it, make an operational check and log the flight in the aircraft records [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(b)]].

final_quiz.q: Which owner record must show, for each applicable AD, the method of compliance, the AD number and revision date, and when the next action is due if it recurs?
options: The pilot's logbook
The registration certificate
The AFM limitations section
The current AD status record under 91.417(a)(2)(v)

final_quiz.q: How long must the owner keep a record of a minor repair under 91.417(a)(1)?
options: Forever, and transfer it at sale
Until the work is repeated or superseded, or 1 year after the work
Until the next annual only
90 days
final_quiz.why: 91.417(b)(1) sets the retention for (a)(1) records [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: An airplane has an auxiliary fuel tank installed in the baggage compartment under part 43. What must be on board?
options: A placard only
A copy of the 100-hour inspection
A copy of the FAA Form 337 authorizing the installation
A special flight permit
final_quiz.why: 91.203(c) requires a copy of the Form 337 on board [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(c)]], and 91.417(d) has the owner keep it there [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(d)]].

final_quiz.q: A registration certificate expires March 31, 2029. When may the holder file for renewal?
options: During the six months before March 31, 2029
Only after March 31, 2029
Any time in the final 30 days
Only at the next annual inspection
final_quiz.why: Renewal is filed with AC Form 8050-1B and the fee during the six months preceding the expiration date [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40(b)]].

final_quiz.q: The owner of a club airplane moved two months ago and never told the FAA. Which rule was missed?
options: 91.417(c), records available to the FAA
47.41(b), notice within 21 days
91.203(b), display of the certificate
47.45, notify the Registry within 30 days
final_quiz.why: Within 30 days after a change in mailing address, the registered owner must notify the Registry in writing [[60:170|14 CFR 47.45]].

final_quiz.q: A registration certificate was issued February 2, 2026. On what date does it expire?
options: February 2, 2033
February 28, 2033
February 28, 2029
February 2, 2029
final_quiz.why: The last day of the month of issue is February 28, 2026. Seven years later is February 28, 2033 [[60:168|14 CFR 47.40(a)]].
